paragraph: Ranking items or individuals by their quantitative attributes often plays a key role in a wide range of domain applications, e.g.,in academia [ 6,31], hiring [ 22], or e-commerce [ 17]. A major underlying assumption of ranking is that a higher ranking reflects a meaningful improvement in utility over lower ranked items. However, if minor modifications to the data result in significant shifts in an item’s position in the ranking, this fundamental assumption is undermined. As a simple example, consider the results of a motorsport event: if the driver finishing 1stdid so with a margin of only 0.2 seconds, the distinction from the runner-up may be practically negligible, whereas a 20-second lead would indicate a clearly superior performance. While the improvement in utility is clear for these simple cases, defining margins between items in more complex settings, such as learning-to-rank (LtR) [50] or rankings based on scores computed by multiple attributes, is not straightforward, as we next illustrate.

In cases where the stable zone is guaranteed to be convex ( e.g.,when the ranking function is based on scores computed by a linear combination of attributes), alternative methods may be used as a drop-in replacement. In particular, [ 16,21] describe efficient algorithms for estimating the volumes of convex polytopes with theoretical guarantees. While these methods offer stronger theoretical guarantees for both accuracy and efficiency when applicable, the Monte Carlo approach is generally efficient and sufficiently accurate for our purposes. Moreover, we note that the convexity assumption does not hold in many practical settings.

In this section, we present an experimental evaluation. We start with two case studies whose goal is to demonstrate the usefulness of our local stability definition. We then study the effect of the sample budgetN, the confidence level δ, and the confidence range ηon the performance of LStability . We examine the performance of Detect-Dense-Region using real and synthetic data, and show the scalability of the algorithm and the usefulness of our proposed optimizations. We conclude with a comparison to the definition of stability that was presented in [3].

Ranking explanations. Beyond ranking stability, the problem of explaining ranking outcomes has been studied extensively [ 1,13–15,20,32]. Many of these works explain rankings by identifying feature importance [ 1,13,14,20,32]. While related to stability, such approaches do not explicitly quantify the margin between tuples in the ranking, as we propose. In [ 13,14], linear scoring functions are fit to a dataset to either match the top- kof a given ranking or put a single tuple among the top-k. The weights of the resulting function may be interpreted as an explanation of feature importance. ShaRP [ 32] adopts Shapley values to explain why a given item ranks the way it does according to the contributions made by each of the individual attributes. Similarly, [ 1] employs existing feature importance methods ( e.g.,LIME [ 35]) to explain rankings. The work of [ 20] exploits monotonicity assumptions to derive importance measures of feature importance. Orthogonally, [15] finds sufficient subsets of attributes (called an abductive explanation) which, when agreed upon, result in the same ordering between tuples.

Robustness verification in ML. Verifying the robustness of machine learning models has been the subject of much recent attention [ 4,11,26,41,47,51,52]. Essentially, robustness quantifies how likely a perturbation to an input will change its prediction [11]. Recent work has focused on probabilistic definitions of robustness, similar to our definition of α-local stability; we refer readers to [52] for a recent survey. Many works ( e.g.,[4,26,41,47,51]) employ a framework similar to ours, leveraging sampling and concentration inequalities to estimate robustness with guarantees on their reliability and accuracy [ 41,47,51]. However, a key difference separates our definition from this line of work: the space of perturbations under consideration. Most often, robustness is considered as a function of an lp-ball [ 4]. This presupposes a cost function on the perturbations enabling the determination of a bound on the maximum cost of changes for which the model is robust. However, our notion of stable zone boundaries replaces this assumed cost function with a weaker assumption: that the cost of a change is monotone non-decreasing. This enables including parts of the stable area which are not included in any lp-ball ( e.g.,the arms of an “L”-shaped stable zone).
